t2.q: Some people believe that artificial intelligence tools in classrooms do more harm than good. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
t2.plan: Artificial intelligence has entered classrooms at remarkable speed, with chatbots now able to explain grammar, solve equations and draft essays in seconds. Some argue that these tools damage learning more than they support it. Although AI can certainly be misused, I largely disagree with this view, because well-managed AI tools make teaching more effective and prepare students for modern working life.

t2.q: In many countries, economic growth is given priority over the protection of the environment. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

This essay will argue that the problem stems mainly from poor diets and inactive lifestyles, and that it can be tackled through a combination of government regulation and changes in schools.

essays.q: The graph below shows the percentage of households with internet access in three countries between 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
paras: The line graph compares the proportion of households with internet access in Canada, Mexico and India over a twenty-year period from 2000 to 2020.

Overall, access to the internet rose steadily in all three countries. Canada had by far the highest level of connection throughout the period, while India, despite starting from the lowest base, saw the most dramatic growth in the second decade.

In 2000, 42% of Canadian households were online, compared with only 6% in Mexico and a negligible 1% in India. The Canadian figure climbed rapidly to 77% by 2008, after which growth slowed considerably, and it eventually levelled off at 93% in 2020.

Mexico and India followed a different pattern. The proportion of connected homes in Mexico increased gradually to 22% in 2008 before accelerating to 60% by the end of the period. India's figure remained very low until 2008, at only 5%, but then rose sharply, more than tripling between 2012 and 2020 to reach 42%. As a result, the gap between Canada and the other two countries narrowed significantly.

essays.q: Some people believe that artificial intelligence tools in classrooms do more harm than good. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
paras: Artificial intelligence has entered classrooms at remarkable speed, with chatbots now able to explain grammar, solve equations and draft essays in seconds. Some argue that these tools damage learning more than they support it. Although AI can certainly be misused, I largely disagree with this view, because well-managed AI tools make teaching more effective and prepare students for modern working life.

The main reason for my position is that AI can provide personalised support that a single teacher cannot. In a class of thirty, a teacher rarely has time to explain a difficult idea to every learner. An AI tutor, by contrast, can adapt explanations to each student's level and give instant feedback, so a pupil struggling with fractions can receive step-by-step hints at home rather than waiting for the next lesson. This, in turn, frees teachers to spend class time on discussion and creative projects.

Furthermore, keeping AI out of schools would leave young people unprepared for a workplace in which these tools are increasingly common. Employers already expect graduates to use AI responsibly, for instance to analyse data or summarise long reports. If teachers show students how to check AI answers, identify errors and acknowledge sources, learners develop critical thinking rather than lose it.

Admittedly, some students use chatbots to complete homework without thinking. However, this problem stems from poor task design rather than from the technology itself: more in-class writing and short oral explanations make copying pointless.

In conclusion, although AI tools may tempt some learners to take shortcuts, I believe that their benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks when teachers guide their use. Schools should therefore teach students to use AI wisely rather than ban it.

essays.q: The chart below shows the average number of hours that first-year and final-year students spend studying each day at five universities. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
paras: The bar chart compares the average number of hours that first-year and final-year students spend studying each day at five universities.

Overall, final-year students studied for longer than first-year students at every institution. Eastbrook and Central recorded the highest study times, whereas Westlake had the lowest figures in both groups of students.

Among first-year students, those at Central studied the most, at five hours a day, followed closely by Eastbrook at 4.5 hours. Students at Southgate and Northfield worked for 3.5 and three hours respectively, while their counterparts at Westlake studied for only 2.5 hours, half the figure for Central.

The pattern for final-year students was broadly similar, although the gaps were wider. Eastbrook's final-years spent six hours a day on their studies, the highest figure in the chart, while Southgate and Central both recorded 5.5 hours. The difference between the two year groups was greatest at Southgate, at two hours, whereas at Westlake and Central it was only half an hour. Westlake again ranked last, with just three hours.

essays.q: Some people believe that schools should spend more time teaching mathematics and numerical skills, while others think that communication skills, such as writing and speaking, will be more important for today's students. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
paras: As the job market changes rapidly, schools face difficult choices about how to divide limited lesson time. Some believe that mathematics and numerical skills deserve greater priority, whereas others argue that the ability to communicate clearly will matter more to today's pupils. In my view, communication skills should receive more attention, although numeracy must remain a core subject.

Those who favour mathematics point out that numerical skills underpin many of the best-paid careers. Engineering, finance and data science all require confident use of statistics and logical reasoning, and the rise of artificial intelligence has made these abilities even more valuable. Moreover, mathematics trains students to solve problems step by step, a habit which is useful in almost every field. From this perspective, reducing maths lessons could limit young people's future opportunities.

On the other hand, supporters of communication skills argue that almost every job, including technical ones, depends on the ability to explain ideas, persuade others and work in a team. A talented programmer who cannot present a project to clients or write a clear report is unlikely to progress far. In addition, now that software performs most routine calculations, the uniquely human skill of communication is becoming harder to replace.

I side with the second view, mainly because communication skills are needed by every student, whereas advanced mathematics is essential only for some. However, the two need not compete: schools could ask pupils to present the results of a statistics project orally, developing both abilities at once.
In conclusion, while numeracy is undeniably important for many careers, I believe communication deserves greater emphasis in today's schools, ideally through lessons that combine the two.

essays.q: The pie charts below show the sources of electricity production in Country Y in 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
paras: The pie charts compare the proportions of electricity generated from five different sources in Country Y in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, the country's energy mix became considerably more balanced over the two decades. Coal lost its dominant position to natural gas, while wind and solar power grew from a negligible share to become a major source of electricity.

In 2000, coal accounted for just over half of all electricity production, more than the other four sources combined. Natural gas was the second largest source, at almost a quarter, whereas nuclear power and hydroelectricity contributed 14% and 8% respectively. Wind and solar energy made up a mere 2% of the total.

By 2020, the share of coal had fallen to 28%, and natural gas had overtaken it to become the leading source, at 31%. The most dramatic change, however, was in renewable energy: the proportion generated by wind and solar rose tenfold to one fifth of the total. By contrast, the figures for nuclear and hydro power remained relatively stable, at 12% and 9% respectively.

essays.q: In many countries, economic growth is given priority over the protection of the environment. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
paras: Many governments, particularly in developing economies, place economic expansion ahead of environmental protection, allowing factories, mines and roads to be built with few restrictions. While this approach can bring rapid improvements in living standards, I believe that its long-term costs clearly outweigh its short-term benefits.

Admittedly, prioritising growth has clear advantages. Rapid industrialisation creates millions of jobs and generates tax revenue that can be spent on schools, hospitals and infrastructure. China's industrial boom in recent decades, for example, lifted hundreds of millions of people out of poverty, albeit at a considerable environmental cost. For a country where many families still lack basic services such as clean water and electricity, such gains are difficult to dismiss.

However, the damage caused by unchecked growth is often severe and, in many cases, irreversible. Air and water pollution lead to respiratory diseases and contaminated food supplies, which place a heavy burden on health systems and reduce workers' productivity. Once a river has been poisoned or a forest cleared, restoring it may take decades and cost far more than preventing the damage in the first place.

Moreover, ignoring the environment can ultimately undermine the economy itself. Climate-related disasters such as floods and droughts destroy crops and infrastructure, and investors are increasingly reluctant to fund polluting industries. Countries that invest early in renewable energy and efficient technology, by contrast, are likely to gain a competitive advantage in the green industries of the future.

In conclusion, although putting growth first may raise incomes in the short term, its health, environmental and economic costs make it a poor long-term strategy. Governments should instead pursue green growth, which balances economic development with environmental sustainability and protects future generations.

essays.q: The table below shows the amount of household waste produced per person and the percentage of household waste recycled in five countries in 2005 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
paras: The table provides data on the amount of household waste produced per person and the percentage of this waste that was recycled in five countries in 2005 and 2020.
Overall, the USA generated by far the most waste per capita in both years, while Germany consistently had the highest recycling rate. Recycling improved in every country, most notably in Poland.

In terms of waste production, each American produced 760 kilograms in 2005, and this figure rose to 810 kilograms in 2020. Germany's output was also high and grew slightly, from 600 to 630 kilograms. Poland produced the least waste in both years, whereas Japan was the only country to achieve a notable reduction, from 410 to 370 kilograms.

As for recycling, Germany recycled more than half of its household waste in 2005 and two thirds by 2020. The most dramatic improvement was in Poland, where the rate soared from 6% to 38%. Turkey also made progress, from just 1% to 12%, while the rates in the USA and Japan rose only marginally, to 35% and 20% respectively.

essays.q: In many countries, the number of overweight children is increasing. What are the reasons for this, and what can be done to tackle the problem?
paras: In many parts of the world, childhood obesity has risen sharply over the past two decades, and doctors warn that overweight children are likely to become unhealthy adults. This essay will argue that the problem stems mainly from poor diets and inactive lifestyles, and that it can be tackled through a combination of government regulation and changes in schools.

The main cause is the widespread availability of cheap processed food. Fast food and sugary drinks are heavily advertised to young people and are often cheaper than fresh fruit and vegetables, so busy parents increasingly rely on them. A second reason is that children now spend far less time being physically active. Instead of playing outside, many spend several hours a day on smartphones and games consoles, which means that they burn far fewer calories than previous generations did.

To address the dietary causes, governments could impose a tax on sugary drinks and ban junk food advertising during children's programmes. Several countries, including the UK and Mexico, have already introduced taxes on sugary drinks, which have encouraged manufacturers to cut the sugar content of their products. The revenue raised could then be used to subsidise healthy school meals.

Schools also have a crucial role to play. If every school provided at least one hour of physical activity a day and taught pupils basic cooking skills, children would not only be fitter but also more likely to make healthy choices as adults. Parents, too, could limit screen time and set an example through their own habits.

In conclusion, childhood obesity is largely the result of unhealthy diets and sedentary lifestyles. Tackling it requires both regulation of the food industry and a greater emphasis on physical activity and nutrition education.

essays.q: The line graph shows the unemployment rate among young people and among all workers in Country Z between 2010 and 2020. The table shows the percentage of workers in four types of job in 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
paras: The line graph shows unemployment rates among people aged 15 to 24 and among all workers in Country Z between 2010 and 2020, while the table compares the proportion of workers in four types of employment in 2010 and 2020.

Overall, youth unemployment was consistently about twice as high as the overall rate, although both followed a similar pattern. Meanwhile, the share of full-time permanent jobs declined, as more people moved into part-time, self-employed and temporary work.

Unemployment among 15- to 24-year-olds rose from 18% in 2010 to a peak of 21% two years later, before falling steadily to a low of 12% in 2018. However, it then climbed back to 17% by 2020. The rate for all workers mirrored this trend at a lower level, peaking at 9.5% in 2012, dropping to 5.5% in 2018 and ending the period at 7.5%.

Turning to the table, full-time permanent positions still accounted for the majority of jobs in 2020, but their share fell by ten percentage points to 58%. By contrast, self-employment rose from 9% to 13%, part-time work from 18% to 21% and temporary or gig work from 5% to 8%.

essays.q: Some companies now offer their employees a four-day working week with no reduction in pay. Why are companies doing this? Is this a positive or negative development?
paras: A growing number of employers, from technology start-ups to large banks, are experimenting with a four-day working week while keeping salaries unchanged. This essay will explain the main reasons for this trend and argue that, on balance, it is a positive development, provided that it is introduced in suitable industries.

Companies are adopting this model primarily to attract and retain skilled staff. In competitive sectors such as software development, talented employees can choose between several job offers, and an extra day off has become a powerful incentive that costs the employer nothing in salary. Another motive is productivity. Trials in several countries, including a widely reported pilot in the UK in 2022, found that many employees completed the same amount of work in fewer hours, partly because they spent less time in unnecessary meetings.

In my view, this shift is largely beneficial. A three-day weekend gives workers more time to rest, spend time with their families and look after their health, which reduces stress and burnout. Rested employees are also less likely to take sick leave, so businesses benefit as well. Furthermore, fewer commuting days mean less traffic congestion and lower emissions in large cities.

Admittedly, the model is not suitable for every sector. Hospitals, schools and shops need staff every day, and squeezing five days of work into four could leave some employees exhausted rather than refreshed. Such organisations would need flexible rotas rather than a single company-wide day off.

In conclusion, companies are introducing a four-day week mainly to attract talent and raise productivity. Although it cannot be applied everywhere, I believe it is a positive development that improves both employees' well-being and business performance.

essays.q: The diagram below shows how instant noodles are manufactured. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.
paras: The diagram illustrates the process by which instant noodles are manufactured, from the storage of flour to the labelling of the finished product.
Overall, there are nine stages in the process, which can be divided into two main phases: the production of the noodles themselves, and the cooking, drying and packaging of the noodle discs.

To begin with, flour is stored in large silos, from where it is transferred to a mixer. Once water and oil have been added, the ingredients are mixed to form a dough, which is then fed through rollers to produce thin sheets. These sheets are subsequently cut into long, thin strips, and in the fifth stage the strips are shaped into round noodle discs.

In the second phase, the discs are cooked in hot oil before being dried and allowed to cool. Each dried disc is then placed in a cup, together with spices and dried vegetables, in the penultimate stage. Finally, the cups are labelled and sealed, ready to be distributed to shops and supermarkets.

essays.q: As English and other global languages spread, many minority languages are losing speakers and may soon disappear. Is this a positive or negative development?
paras: As English and a handful of other global languages spread through education, business and the internet, many smaller languages are losing speakers, and linguists warn that a large number of the world's languages are now endangered. Although a shared global language brings practical benefits, I believe the loss of minority languages is, overall, a negative development.

It is true that the dominance of a few global languages has advantages. When people share a common language, international trade, scientific cooperation and travel become far easier. A young person from a small community who learns English, for instance, gains access to online courses, global job markets and a vast body of information. From a purely economic perspective, therefore, abandoning a local language may seem a rational choice.

However, a language is far more than a tool for communication. Each language carries a community's history, oral literature and traditional knowledge, such as local names for medicinal plants or farming methods adapted to a particular climate. When the last speakers die, this knowledge usually disappears with them, and future generations lose an important link to their identity.

Moreover, this loss is unnecessary, because people do not have to choose between a global language and their mother tongue. In Uzbekistan, for example, many young people speak Uzbek at home, Russian in some workplaces and English online, which shows that several languages can comfortably coexist. Schools and the media can support this balance by offering bilingual education and content in local languages.

In conclusion, while global languages make communication more efficient, the disappearance of smaller languages represents an irreversible cultural loss. Governments and communities should therefore encourage bilingualism, so that people can enjoy the benefits of both.

essays.q: The maps below show the centre of the town of Halden in 2005 and today. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
paras: The two maps illustrate how the centre of Halden has changed between 2005 and the present day.

Overall, the town centre has been transformed from a partly industrial area into a more commercial and residential space, with a greater emphasis on pedestrians and public transport. The houses in the south-west are the only feature that has remained unchanged.

On the western side of Main Street, the factory beside the river has been demolished and replaced by apartments, while the car park to the south of it has been converted into a shopping centre. Further south, the residential area has been left as it was.

East of Main Street, the open-air market square has been pedestrianised and now has a number of cafés. The park to the south has been reduced to roughly half its original size to make way for a new car park, and in the south-east the bus station has been replaced by a tram stop. Finally, a footbridge has been built across the river in the north.

essays.q: Some people prefer to shop in large shopping centres, while others prefer local markets and small shops. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
paras: In many cities, including Tashkent, modern shopping malls now stand alongside traditional bazaars and neighbourhood shops. While some consumers favour the convenience of large shopping centres, others remain loyal to local markets. In my opinion, both have a place, but local markets offer greater long-term benefits to communities and therefore deserve support.

Those who prefer shopping centres point to convenience and comfort. A modern mall brings supermarkets, clothing stores, restaurants and cinemas together under one roof, so a family can complete a week's shopping and enjoy an evening out in a single trip. Malls are also air-conditioned in summer and heated in winter, and prices are clearly displayed, which many shoppers find reassuring.

On the other hand, supporters of local markets argue that they offer fresher produce and a more personal experience. Fruit and vegetables at a bazaar often come directly from nearby farms, so they tend to be cheaper and have travelled a shorter distance. Moreover, buyers can negotiate prices and build relationships with stallholders over many years, which creates a sense of community that impersonal chain stores rarely provide.

I lean towards the second view, mainly for economic reasons. Money spent at a small, family-run business tends to stay in the local economy, supporting farmers and creating jobs, whereas a large share of the profits made by international chains goes elsewhere. If local markets disappeared, city centres would also lose much of their character.

In conclusion, shopping centres offer unmatched convenience, but local markets bring fresher food, stronger communities and lasting benefits to the local economy. For this reason, city authorities should protect and modernise traditional markets rather than allow malls to replace them.

essays.q: The graph below shows the percentage of adults in one country who regularly got news from four sources between 2000 and 2025, with projections to 2035. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
paras: The line graph shows the percentage of adults who regularly obtained news from four different sources between 2000 and 2025, with projections up to 2035.

Overall, online news has risen dramatically and is expected to become by far the most popular source, whereas all three traditional media have declined and are predicted to continue falling. Newspapers have experienced the steepest decline.

In 2000, television was the leading source of news, used by 78% of adults, followed by newspapers at 62%, while only 8% of people got their news online. However, online use grew rapidly, overtaking newspapers in the early 2010s and television shortly before 2020, and it reached 72% in 2025. This figure is projected to rise further to 85% by 2035.

By contrast, the proportion of people relying on television fell steadily to 50% in 2025 and is forecast to drop to 40% by 2035. Newspaper readership is expected to shrink even more sharply, from 18% to just 8%, making it the least used source. Radio, meanwhile, has declined only gradually and is set to stabilise at around a quarter of adults.

essays.q: In the developed world, average life expectancy is increasing. What problems will this cause for individuals and society? Suggest some measures that could be taken to reduce the impact of ageing populations.
paras: Thanks to advances in medicine and better living conditions, people in developed countries are living considerably longer than previous generations. While this is a remarkable achievement, it creates serious challenges for both individuals and society. This essay will examine these problems and suggest measures to reduce their impact.

For individuals, the main difficulty is financial. Many people now spend twenty years or more in retirement, and their savings and state pensions are often insufficient to support them for so long. In addition, a longer life does not always mean a healthier one; many elderly people live with chronic conditions such as dementia or arthritis, which can lead to social isolation and dependence on relatives who may themselves be working full-time.

At the level of society, an ageing population puts enormous strain on public finances. As the proportion of retirees grows, a shrinking workforce must pay for rising pension and healthcare costs. Japan, where nearly 30% of the population is now aged 65 or over, illustrates how labour shortages and growing medical spending can slow economic growth.

Several measures could ease these pressures. Firstly, governments could gradually raise the retirement age and encourage flexible part-time work for older people, allowing them to stay active and continue paying taxes. Secondly, greater investment in preventive healthcare, such as regular check-ups and community exercise programmes, would help people remain healthy for longer and reduce the burden on hospitals. Finally, workplace pension schemes could be made compulsory so that workers save adequately from an early age.

In conclusion, rising life expectancy brings financial insecurity and health problems for individuals and puts pressure on public services. However, later retirement, preventive healthcare and better pension planning could significantly reduce these effects.

essays.q: The diagram below shows the life cycle of the silkworm and the production of silk. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.
paras: The diagram illustrates the life cycle of the silkworm and shows how silk is obtained from its cocoons.

Overall, the silkworm passes through four main stages, developing from an egg into a larva, a pupa and finally an adult moth, in a continuous cycle. At the cocoon stage, however, some cocoons are taken and processed by humans to produce raw silk.

The cycle begins when a female moth lays between 300 and 500 eggs on a mulberry leaf. After about ten days, the eggs hatch into larvae, commonly known as silkworms, which feed on mulberry leaves for four to six weeks. Once fully grown, each larva spends approximately three days spinning a cocoon of silk thread.

Inside the cocoon, the silkworm develops into a pupa over a period of two to three weeks. It then emerges as an adult moth, which lives for only around a week, during which time it mates and lays eggs, so the cycle starts again. Meanwhile, some of the cocoons are boiled so that the thread can be unwound to make raw silk.

essays.q: Nowadays, more and more people get their news from social media rather than from newspapers or television. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this?
paras: Social media platforms have become the main source of news for many people, particularly the young, who increasingly scroll through feeds instead of buying newspapers or watching evening bulletins. This shift has both clear benefits and significant drawbacks, which this essay will discuss.

The most obvious advantage is speed. Breaking news, such as an earthquake or an election result, often appears on social media within minutes, sometimes posted by eyewitnesses before journalists arrive. Social media also gives a voice to ordinary people and smaller communities whose concerns are often ignored by the mainstream media. In addition, news is free and can be accessed anywhere on a smartphone, which makes information available to people who cannot afford newspaper subscriptions.

However, these benefits come at a cost. The main disadvantage is the rapid spread of misinformation. Because anyone can publish content without checking facts, false stories and edited videos can reach millions of users before they are corrected. During the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, misleading claims about vaccines circulated widely online and may have discouraged some people from being vaccinated.

Another drawback is that social media algorithms tend to show users content that matches their existing views. Over time, this can create so-called echo chambers, in which people rarely encounter opposing opinions and may become more polarised. Moreover, short posts and headlines encourage superficial reading, so users may feel well informed while understanding complex issues only partially.

In conclusion, social media makes news faster, cheaper and more inclusive, but it also spreads misinformation and narrows the range of views people see. To enjoy the benefits while limiting the risks, users need strong media literacy, and platforms should take greater responsibility for the content they promote.

essays.q: The maps below show an industrial area in the town of Riverton at present and the planned future development of the area. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
paras: The maps show an industrial area in the town of Riverton at present and the changes that are planned for its future development.

Overall, the area is set to be transformed from an industrial zone into a residential and community district, with all of the existing industrial buildings removed. In addition, transport links and green space are to be improved.

West of the main road, the factories in the north are to be demolished to make way for a housing estate, while the warehouses to the south will be replaced by a school and a community centre. On the eastern side, the factory will be replaced by offices and shops, and the lorry park below it is planned to become another area of housing.

Two further changes are proposed at the edges of the site. Along the river in the south, a park with a cycle path will be created, stretching across the whole width of the area. In the north, a new railway station will be built on the existing line, just to the east of the main road.

essays.q: In many countries, young adults are living with their parents for longer than in the past. Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?
paras: In many countries, including Uzbekistan, it is increasingly common for people in their twenties and even thirties to remain in the family home. This essay will argue that the trend is driven mainly by economic pressures and longer education, and that its effects are, on the whole, more positive than negative.

The most important reason is the rising cost of independent living. In large cities, rents and property prices have increased far faster than starting salaries, so many young graduates simply cannot afford a flat of their own. A second factor is that young people now spend longer in education; a student who completes a master's degree may not earn a full salary until the age of 25 or later. In some cultures, moreover, it has always been normal for unmarried children to live with their parents.

In my view, this development is largely positive. Living at home allows young adults to save money for a deposit on a home or to start a business, rather than spending most of their income on rent. It can also strengthen family ties: grown-up children can support parents as they age, while parents can offer advice and emotional support during a stressful stage of life.

Admittedly, there are drawbacks. Young people who rely on their parents for too long may develop independence more slowly, for example in managing a household budget. Overcrowding can also create tension, particularly in small apartments. However, these problems can be reduced if young adults contribute to household costs and take on responsibilities at home.

In conclusion, young adults are staying with their parents longer mainly because of high housing costs and extended education. Although the trend may delay independence, I believe that its financial and family benefits make it a broadly positive development.
The line graph illustrates changes in the proportion of the Australian workforce employed in five industries over a fifty-year period from 1962 to 2012.

Overall, manufacturing, which was by far the largest employer in 1962, declined dramatically, as did agriculture, whereas health care and professional services grew steadily. By the end of the period, retail trade and health care had become the two largest sectors.

In 1962, manufacturing accounted for 26% of all workers, more than twice the figure for retail trade (12%) and agriculture (11%). Over the following five decades, the manufacturing share fell continuously, dropping below that of retail in the late 1980s and reaching just 8% in 2012. Agriculture followed a similar downward path, shrinking to only 3% of the workforce.

By contrast, health care expanded steadily from 5% to 12%, ending the period level with retail trade, which had risen gradually to a peak of 15% in 1992 and 2002 before falling back to 12%. Professional services also more than tripled, from 3% to 9.5%, overtaking agriculture in the mid-1980s and manufacturing towards the end of the period.

As cities grow and car ownership rises, governments must decide how to spend limited transport budgets. Some argue that public transport should receive priority over new roads. I largely agree with this view, since public transport moves more people at a lower cost to society, although some road investment remains necessary.

The main reason is that new roads rarely solve congestion for long. When a motorway is widened, journeys become faster at first, which encourages more people to drive, and within a few years the traffic returns, a phenomenon known as induced demand. A modern metro or bus rapid transit line, by contrast, can carry tens of thousands of passengers an hour while using far less space. The recent expansion of the Tashkent metro, for instance, has given residents of outlying districts a fast alternative to crowded roads.

Furthermore, investing in public transport brings environmental and social benefits. Buses and trains produce considerably lower emissions per passenger than private cars, which helps cities tackle air pollution. They also give students, older people and low-income workers, many of whom cannot afford a car, affordable access to jobs and education.

Admittedly, roads cannot be ignored entirely. Rural areas with small populations are poorly suited to rail networks, and buses themselves need well-maintained roads. Freight transport also depends on a reliable road system. However, these needs can usually be met by repairing existing roads rather than building new ones.

In conclusion, while some spending on roads is unavoidable, I believe that governments should direct most new transport investment towards public transport, as it offers a more lasting solution to congestion and brings wider benefits to society.
